blocks.text: Given a string, the Longest Palindromic Substring problem asks for the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards. It looks simple, but it is one of the most commonly mis-solved problems in interviews because the natural first approaches are quadratic or worse.
Manacher's Algorithm solves it in O(n) time, a striking result compared to a brute force check at O(n^3) or the popular expand around center approach at O(n^2).

The trick is not a new way to check palindromes. It is a way to reuse work already done for palindromes found earlier in the string, so that no character ends up compared more times than necessary across the entire scan.

items: Brute force: check every substring for the palindrome property, O(n^3)
Expand around center: try every possible center and grow outward, O(n^2)
Manacher's Algorithm: a single linear pass that reuses previously computed palindrome radii, O(n)

blocks.text: This document builds up to Manacher's Algorithm in order: the naive approaches first, then the transformation that unifies odd and even length palindromes, then the core P array, and finally the mirror trick that makes the whole scan linear.
For s = "babad", both "bab" and "aba" are valid answers, since both are palindromes of the maximum possible length, 3. Either one may be returned.
The brute force approach checks every one of the O(n^2) substrings and verifies the palindrome property in O(n) per check, giving O(n^3) overall.

A dynamic programming table trims the check to O(1) per substring by reusing whether the inner substring is already known to be a palindrome, bringing the total down to O(n^2) time, but it still needs O(n^2) space to store the table.

items: Brute force substring check: O(n^3) time, O(1) extra space
Dynamic programming table: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
Expand around center: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space
Manacher's Algorithm: O(n) time, O(n) space

blocks.text: Expand around center is the approach most people reach for first, since it needs no extra memory. It is also the direct ancestor of Manacher's Algorithm, so it is worth walking through before adding the linear time trick.

content.title: 2. Expand Around Center: The O(n^2) Approach

blocks.text: The idea is direct: treat every index as the center of a possible palindrome, and grow outward while the characters on both sides keep matching. The widest successful expansion at any center is the longest palindrome centered there.

A single index only covers odd length palindromes, where there is one middle character. Even length palindromes, where the middle is a pair of matching characters, need a second kind of center sitting between two adjacent indices. Both kinds must be tried at every position.

There are 2n-1 possible centers, n for odd length and n-1 for even length, and each expansion can take O(n) time in the worst case, for example a string made entirely of one repeated character. That gives O(n^2) overall.

This is a solid interview answer on its own, but it wastes information. Expanding around center i never looks at what was already learned while expanding around center i-1, even when the two palindromes overlap heavily. Manacher's Algorithm keeps the expand outward spirit but adds bookkeeping so overlapping work is never repeated.

content.title: 3. The Even Length Problem and the Separator Trick

blocks.text: The expand around center code above needed two separate expansion calls per index, one for odd length and one for even length, because a single index cannot be the exact center of an even length palindrome. Manacher's Algorithm removes this split entirely with a single upfront transformation of the string.

The idea: insert a unique separator character, conventionally #, between every pair of adjacent characters and at both ends of the string. After this transformation, every palindrome, in the transformed string, has odd length with a single well defined center.
For s = "aba", the transformed string is t = "#a#b#a#".

blocks.caption: The transformed string #a#b#a#, every substring now has odd length with a single center.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785250309291-154719188.png
blocks.alt: Separator trick transforms aba into hash-a-hash-b-hash-a-hash

blocks.text: Why the transformation works

A separator character can only ever match another separator character during expansion, since it never appears as a real character in the input. This has two consequences: any palindrome that was odd length in the original string stays centered on the same real character, just padded with matching separators on both sides, and any palindrome that was even length in the original string becomes centered exactly on the separator that used to sit between its two middle characters.

items: Original even length palindrome: "abba"
Transformed: "#a#b#b#a#"
The center is now the separator between the two 'b' characters, and the palindrome around it reads the same on both sides

blocks.text: A second useful consequence: if the original string s has length n, the transformed string t always has length 2n+1, which is odd. There is never an ambiguous two character center to handle again, every index in t has exactly one center to consider.

The separator only has to satisfy one property: it must not appear anywhere in the input alphabet, so it can never accidentally match a real character. # works for most problems since inputs are usually letters or digits, but any character outside the input's alphabet is a valid choice.

content.title: 4. The P Array: Radius of the Longest Palindrome at Each Center

blocks.text: Once the string is transformed, define an array P where P[i] is the radius of the longest palindrome centered at index i in t, meaning the number of characters that match symmetrically outward from i before a mismatch or a string boundary is hit.
Formally, P[i] is the largest r such that t[i-r..i+r] is a palindrome and stays within the bounds of t.

blocks.caption: The radius P[3]=3 at the center index 3, spanning three matching characters on each side.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785250311135-878823438.png
blocks.alt: P array radius of the longest palindrome centered at an index

blocks.text: Two conversion formulas connect P directly back to the original string s, and they hold for every index i regardless of whether i sits on a real character or a separator:

items: Length of the palindrome in s: P[i]
Start index of the palindrome in s: (i-P[i])/2

blocks.text: This is exactly why the separator transformation removes the odd versus even special case for good: both kinds of palindrome are read off the same P array with the same two formulas, there is nothing left to branch on.

Once P is filled in for every index, the answer to Longest Palindromic Substring is just the index holding the largest P value, converted back with the two formulas above. The remaining question is how to fill P in O(n) total time instead of O(n^2).

content.title: 5. The Key Insight: Reusing Previous Work

blocks.text: Filling P one index at a time by brute force expansion is still O(n^2) in the worst case, even on the transformed string, for example a string of all identical characters produces long expansions at nearly every center. The linear time bound comes from a second idea layered on top of expansion: reusing the radius already computed for a mirror position.

While scanning t left to right, the algorithm keeps two running values: C, the center of whichever palindrome currently reaches furthest to the right, and R, that palindrome's right boundary, R = C+P[C].

Suppose the scan has reached index i, and i falls strictly inside the current palindrome, meaning i<R. Because that palindrome is symmetric around C, there is a mirror position i' = 2*C-i on the opposite side of C, and by symmetry, the palindrome structure already known around i' also exists, reflected, around i, at least up to the boundary R.
This lets P[i] start from min(R-i, P[i']) instead of starting from 0. Two cases follow from that minimum:

items: If P[i'] is strictly smaller than R-i, the mirrored palindrome around i' fits entirely inside the known palindrome around C. By symmetry, P[i] is exactly P[i'], and no expansion at i is needed at all.

If P[i'] is greater than or equal to R-i, the mirrored palindrome touches or would exceed the known boundary R. Symmetry is only guaranteed up to R, so the algorithm must still attempt to expand past R, character by character, to find out if the palindrome actually continues further.

blocks.text: If i is at or past the current boundary, i>=R, there is no useful mirror information yet, and the algorithm falls back to plain expansion starting from radius 0, exactly like the O(n^2) approach, just for that one position.

After P[i] is finalized, if the palindrome at i reaches past the current boundary, i+P[i]>R, then C and R are updated to i and i+P[i], so the newest, furthest reaching palindrome becomes the reference for every later position.

blocks.caption: The mirror position i' reflects known structure around center C out to the current position i, up to right boundary R.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785250312773-801240807.png
blocks.alt: Mirror trick reuses previous palindrome radius via center and boundary

blocks.text: The mirror trick never produces a wrong answer by itself, it only ever supplies a safe starting guess for P[i]. Any growth beyond what the mirror already guarantees is always verified character by character before being accepted.

Trace the algorithm on s = "abaaba". This string is chosen because it is itself a full palindrome of even length 6, and it also contains a shorter odd length palindrome "aba", so both the plain expansion case and both mirror trick cases show up in a single pass.
After transformation, t = "#a#b#a#a#b#a#", which has length 13, indices 0 through 12.
Scanning left to right and maintaining C, the center of the rightmost known palindrome, and R, its right boundary:

codes.javascript:
i=0..2 : P=0,1,0   (C=R=0 initially, no mirror info yet)

i=3 (t[3]='b'): i >= R, expand from scratch
  radius grows to 3 -> t[0..6] = "#a#b#a#" is a palindrome
  P[3] = 3; since 3+3=6 > R(0), update C=3, R=6

i=4: i < R(6), mirror = 2*3-4 = 2, P[2]=0, R-i=2, min(0,2)=0
  expand fails immediately -> P[4] = 0

i=5: i < R(6), mirror = 2*3-5 = 1, P[1]=1, R-i=1, min(1,1)=1 (tie, must verify)
  try r=2: t[3]='b' vs t[7]='a' -> mismatch -> P[5] = 1

i=6 (t[6]='#'): i >= R(6), expand from scratch
  radius grows all the way to 6 -> t[0..12] is a palindrome (the whole string)
  P[6] = 6; since 6+6=12 > R(6), update C=6, R=12

i=7: i < R(12), mirror = 2*6-7 = 5, P[5]=1, R-i=5, min(1,5)=1 (P[mirror] < R-i, exact)
  P[7] = 1, no expansion attempted at all

i=8: mirror = 4, P[4]=0, R-i=4, min(0,4)=0 (exact) -> P[8] = 0, no expansion attempted

i=9: mirror = 3, P[3]=3, R-i=3 (tie, must verify)
  try r=4: t[5]='a' vs t[13] -> out of bounds -> P[9] = 3

i=10: mirror = 2, P[2]=0, R-i=2 (exact) -> P[10] = 0, no expansion attempted

i=11: mirror = 1, P[1]=1, R-i=1 (tie, must verify)
  try r=2: t[9]='b' vs t[13] -> out of bounds -> P[11] = 1

i=12: i >= R(12), boundary -> P[12] = 0

blocks.text: The final array is P = [0,1,0,3,0,1,6,1,0,3,0,1,0]. Its maximum value is 6, at index 6.
Converting back: start = (6-6)/2 = 0 and length = P[6] = 6, giving s[0..5] = "abaaba", the entire string, which is correct since "abaaba" is itself a palindrome.

Three moments in this trace are worth pausing on. At i=7, i=8 and i=10, the mirror value was accepted outright with zero character comparisons. At i=9 and i=11, the mirror value touched the boundary exactly, forcing one verification step that failed immediately at the edge of the string. At i=3 and i=6, there was no useful mirror yet, so the algorithm fell back to full expansion. This mix, mostly free reuse with occasional bounded verification, is exactly why the total work across the whole string stays linear.
A complete, from scratch implementation, including the transformation and the conversion back to the original string:
Calling longestPalindrome(s) directly returns the longest palindromic substring of s. The transformation, the P array, and the back conversion are all handled inside this one function.
The claim is O(n) time overall, even though the inner while loop that expands P[i] looks, at first glance, like it could redo O(n) work at every single index in the worst case.
Why the bound holds

The key is that every character comparison inside the expansion loop that actually succeeds (both sides match, so the radius grows by one) also increases R by exactly one, because expansion is only ever continued past what the mirror trick already guaranteed, which means the frontier of newly examined characters is always exactly at R. Since R starts at 0, only ever moves rightward, and cannot exceed n, the total number of successful expansion steps across the entire scan is bounded by n.

Every index also contributes at most one failed comparison, the single character comparison that stops its expansion loop. That is another O(n) across the whole scan. Everything else, the mirror lookup and the min computation, is O(1) per index.

items: Time: O(n), a single linear pass, O(1) amortized work per index
Space: O(n), for the transformed string t and the P array, both roughly double the length of the original string

blocks.text: This makes Manacher's Algorithm the only approach in this family that is linear in both the size of the input and the total work performed, compared to O(n^3) brute force, O(n^2) time and space dynamic programming, and O(n^2) time expand around center.
A handful of mistakes account for most bugs in Manacher's Algorithm implementations:

items: Skipping the separator transformation and trying to run the P array logic directly on the original string. This breaks the single center assumption that makes even length palindromes work at all.
Off by one errors converting a P value back to a substring. The correct formulas are length = P[i] and start = (i-P[i])/2 in the original string, not i/2 or P[i]/2.

Forgetting to bound expansion properly when the mirror position's palindrome touches or exceeds the current right boundary, the tie case where P[i']>=R-i. The algorithm must still attempt to expand past R and verify character by character, it cannot simply copy P[i'] as the final answer.

Not updating C and R after computing P[i]. If the new palindrome extends past R, the boundary must move forward, otherwise later positions lose the benefit of the mirror trick entirely and the algorithm silently degrades toward O(n^2).
Choosing a separator character that can appear in the input, which lets it accidentally match a real character and corrupts palindrome boundaries.
Missing bounds checks in the expansion loop, forgetting to test both i-P[i]-1>=0 and i+P[i]+1<n before comparing characters, which reads out of bounds at the ends of the transformed string.
Easy Palindromic Substrings (LC 647): count every palindromic substring. The P array gives this directly, each P[i] contributes ceil(P[i]/2) palindromes centered at i.
Medium Longest Palindromic Substring (LC 5): the canonical Manacher's Algorithm problem.
Medium Longest Palindromic Subsequence (LC 516): a different problem entirely, subsequence rather than substring, solved with interval dynamic programming. Manacher's Algorithm does not apply here.

Hard Shortest Palindrome (LC 214): add the fewest characters in front of a string to make the whole thing a palindrome. A related but distinct problem, usually solved with KMP's failure function or the Z algorithm rather than Manacher's Algorithm.

Hard Palindrome Pairs (LC 336): find pairs of words that concatenate into a palindrome. Typically solved with hashing or a trie, not Manacher's Algorithm, even though the vocabulary of centers and mirroring is conceptually related.

blocks.text: It helps to know the boundary of what Manacher's Algorithm actually solves: it finds palindromic structure centered at every position in one string. Problems about repeated prefixes, like Shortest Palindrome, lean on KMP or the Z algorithm instead, and problems about subsequences or multiple strings usually lean on dynamic programming or hashing.

items: Can you explain why the separator transformation makes every palindrome odd length, and why that removes the need to special case even length palindromes?
Can you state what P[i] means, and derive length = P[i] and start = (i-P[i])/2 to convert back to the original string?
Can you explain the mirror trick: why P[i] can start from min(R-i, P[i']), and why the algorithm must still verify character by character when P[i']>=R-i?
Can you give the amortized argument for why the total work stays O(n) despite the expansion loop inside the main scan?
Can you implement the full algorithm, transformation, P array, and the back conversion, from scratch in under 10 minutes?
Do you know when Manacher's Algorithm does not apply, for example Longest Palindromic Subsequence or Shortest Palindrome, and what to reach for instead?
